result.markdown: --- title: "Smoothing" subtitle: "fit_scattered and the Gaussian against the smoothing splines of BSplineKit.jl and Dierckx.jl and the polynomial regression of FastChebInterp.jl" engine: julia --- Recovering a signal from noisy samples on a uniform grid: `fit_scattered`, which chooses its smoothing by generalized cross-validation, and the package's Gaussian kernel against the cubic smoothing spline of BSplineKit.jl, the quintic FITPACK smoothing spline of Dierckx.jl and the least-squares Chebyshev polynomial of FastChebInterp.jl. Each of those four has a parameter the user must choose — the width `B`, the penalty `λ`, the residual budget `s`, the degree — so each is given the value that minimises the error against the signal, found by searching for it: an oracle no user has. `fit_scattered` is told nothing. Accuracy against noise level and signal frequency, then time, then the two together as the samples grow. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Packages and the methods"} using ConvolutionInterpolations import BSplineKit import Dierckx import FastChebInterp using Chairmarks, Printf, Random, CairoMakie rms(v) = sqrt(sum(abs2, v) / length(v)) # root mean square, the error measure throughout logrange10(a, b, n) = exp10.(range(log10(a), log10(b), length = n)) # n values from a to b, logarithmically spaced # the smoothing of a noisy sine as a function of the smoothing parameter p: each method maps # (x, y, p) to the smoothed values on the grid x gaussian(x, y, B) = convolution_smooth(x, y, B) # the package's Gaussian kernel, width B in grid spacings bsk(x, y, λ) = BSplineKit.fit(BSplineKit.BSplineOrder(4), x, y, λ).(x) # the cubic smoothing spline, penalty weight λ # the quintic FITPACK spline, residual budget s; FITPACK errors when s is smaller than it can reach, # which the oracle search treats as a failed trial (infinite error) rather than a failure of the page dierckx(x, y, s) = try Dierckx.Spline1D(collect(x), y; k = 5, s = s).(x) catch fill(Inf, length(x)) end cheb(x, y, d) = FastChebInterp.chebregression(collect(x), y, d).(x) # the least-squares Chebyshev polynomial of degree d # fit_scattered takes the knots as a matrix of points and returns a fitted grid; the fitted # values on the data grid come from the interpolant built on that grid with the kernel the fit used function fitted(x, y) knots, vals, _ = fit_scattered(reshape(collect(x), 1, :), y; mode = :smooth, grid = :adaptive) # the smoothing is chosen by cross-validation convolution_interpolation(knots, vals; kernel = :b5).(x) end # the oracle: the parameter in the range that gives the smallest error against the signal function oracle(method, x, y, clean, range) errs = [rms(method(x, y, p) .- clean) for p in range] i = argmin(errs) (p = range[i], err = errs[i]) end # the parameter ranges searched; the splines' ranges scale with the data, so they are functions of n and σ Brange(n) = (400 / n)^2 .* logrange10(0.005, 2.0, 25) # Gaussian widths in grid spacings, scaled so the width in x is the same on every grid λrange = logrange10(1e-9, 1e2, 34) # penalty weights, from interpolation to a straight line srange(n, σ) = n * σ^2 .* logrange10(0.05, 20.0, 27) # residual budgets around the expected residual n σ² drange(n) = 2:2:min(160, n - 1) # polynomial degrees, at most the number of samples allows # one noise realisation, drawn once on the finest grid of the page; every grid whose spacing is a # multiple of the finest one takes its noise from it, so that refining the grid changes only the # samples, not the noise. A grid that does not nest in the finest one gets its own draw. const NMAX = 6401 const NOISE = randn(MersenneTwister(1), NMAX) function noise(n) if (NMAX - 1) % (n - 1) == 0 NOISE[1:(NMAX - 1) ÷ (n - 1):end] # every stride-th value of the shared realisation else randn(MersenneTwister(1), n) end end # the test signal: a sine with k cycles over [0, 2π], sampled at n points with noise of standard deviation σ function signal(n, k, σ) x = range(0, 2π, length = n) clean = sin.(k .* x) noisy = clean .+ σ .* noise(n) (x = x, clean = clean, noisy = noisy) end # the five errors of one test case, the fit untuned and the others at their oracle parameter function errors(n, k, σ) x, clean, noisy = signal(n, k, σ) (fit = rms(fitted(x, noisy) .- clean), gaussian = oracle(gaussian, x, noisy, clean, Brange(n)).err, bsk = oracle(bsk, x, noisy, clean, λrange).err, dierckx = oracle(dierckx, x, noisy, clean, srange(n, σ)).err, cheb = oracle(cheb, x, noisy, clean, drange(n)).err) end names = (fit = "fit_scattered (untuned)", gaussian = "Gaussian (oracle B)", bsk = "BSplineKit cubic (oracle λ)", dierckx = "Dierckx k=5 (oracle s)", cheb = "FastChebInterp (oracle degree)"); ``` ::: ## Noise level and signal frequency Four hundred samples. Left, three cycles of the sine and the noise standard deviation growing from one percent of the amplitude to a third of it; right, the noise fixed at a tenth and the number of cycles growing until the grid has about thirteen points per cycle. The error is the root mean square against the signal on the data grid; the data's own error, which smoothing should improve on, is the noise standard deviation. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The noise and frequency studies"} n = 401 # one more than 400, so the grid nests in the finest one of the page σs = (0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3) # noise levels at k = 3 ks = (1, 3, 10, 30) # cycles at σ = 0.1 by_noise = [errors(n, 3, σ) for σ in σs] by_freq = [errors(n, k, 0.1) for k in ks] fig = Figure(size = (800, 380)) ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "noise standard deviation σ", ylabel = "rms error", title = "3 cycles") ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "cycles over the interval", title = "σ = 0.1") for key in keys(names) scatterlines!(ax1, collect(σs), [e[key] for e in by_noise]; markersize = 8, label = names[key]) scatterlines!(ax2, collect(ks), [e[key] for e in by_freq]; markersize = 8) end lines!(ax1, collect(σs), collect(σs); color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "the noise itself") hlines!(ax2, [0.1]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash) Legend(fig[2, 1:2], ax1; orientation = :horizontal, nbanks = 2) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | rms error, 3 cycles | σ = 0.01 | σ = 0.03 | σ = 0.1 | σ = 0.3 | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | fit_scattered (untuned) | 0.0024 | 0.0069 | 0.0230 | 0.0683 | | Gaussian (oracle B) | 0.0049 | 0.0120 | 0.0321 | 0.0796 | | BSplineKit cubic (oracle λ) | 0.0032 | 0.0085 | 0.0249 | 0.0633 | | Dierckx k=5 (oracle s) | 0.0036 | 0.0093 | 0.0306 | 0.1002 | | FastChebInterp (oracle degree) | 0.0019 | 0.0056 | 0.0181 | 0.0536 | | rms error, σ = 0.1 | 1 cycles | 3 cycles | 10 cycles | 30 cycles | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | fit_scattered (untuned) | 0.0137 | 0.0230 | 0.0327 | 0.0544 | | Gaussian (oracle B) | 0.0178 | 0.0321 | 0.0493 | 0.0725 | | BSplineKit cubic (oracle λ) | 0.0139 | 0.0249 | 0.0383 | 0.0584 | | Dierckx k=5 (oracle s) | 0.0127 | 0.0306 | 0.0394 | 0.0617 | | FastChebInterp (oracle degree) | 0.0139 | 0.0181 | 0.0346 | 0.0508 | The tuned rows are the best each method can do, found by looking at the answer; the fit's row is what it does on its own. Even so the fit is ahead of the Gaussian and the splines nearly everywhere, and level with the Chebyshev polynomial — a global fit, the ideal smoother for a sine — from three cycles up. Its loss at one cycle is GCV's: on a short series of a very smooth signal the criterion's minimum is shallow and it settles on too little smoothing. What a user gets from the other methods is a hand-chosen parameter, which lands somewhere above each oracle row. ## Setup The time to produce the smoothed values on the grid, for the four hundred samples above and for ten thousand, each method at its parameter from the first study. The fit's time includes the cross-validation that chooses its parameter; the other three are timed at a parameter already known, so the search that found it is not in their times. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The timings"} fmt(t) = t < 1e-6 ? @sprintf("%.0f ns", 1e9 * t) : t < 1e-3 ? @sprintf("%.1f μs", 1e6 * t) : t < 1 ? @sprintf("%.2f ms", 1e3 * t) : @sprintf("%.2f s", t) function timings(n) x, clean, noisy = signal(n, 3, 0.1) B = oracle(gaussian, x, noisy, clean, Brange(n)).p λ = oracle(bsk, x, noisy, clean, λrange).p s = oracle(dierckx, x, noisy, clean, srange(n, 0.1)).p d = oracle(cheb, x, noisy, clean, drange(n)).p (fit = (@b fitted($x, $noisy)).time, gaussian = (@b gaussian($x, $noisy, $B)).time, bsk = (@b bsk($x, $noisy, $λ)).time, dierckx = (@b dierckx($x, $noisy, $s)).time, cheb = (@b cheb($x, $noisy, $d)).time) end t400 = timings(401) t10k = timings(10_000); ``` ::: | | 401 samples | 10 000 samples | |:--|--:|--:| | fit_scattered (untuned) | 115.80 ms | 1.06 s | | Gaussian (oracle B) | 7.6 μs | 2.97 ms | | BSplineKit cubic (oracle λ) | 525.1 μs | 256.99 ms | | Dierckx k=5 (oracle s) | 581.8 μs | 13.04 ms | | FastChebInterp (oracle degree) | 29.5 μs | 1.25 ms | The Gaussian is a pass over the data, the polynomial a small least-squares problem, the splines a banded solve; the fit solves a sparse system once per trial value of its smoothing parameter, first on a grid as fine as the data and then on the coarse grid the smoothing needs, so its cost is the price of not having to choose. Where the parameter is known, the Gaussian is the fast path, and in many dimensions the only feasible one. ## Time to accuracy With noise, the error falls with the number of samples for every method, so the question of which reaches a given accuracy in the least time has the same shape as on the interpolation page. Three cycles, noise of a tenth, and the number of samples doubling; each method's time to produce the smoothed values on its grid against its error there. The tuned methods are again at their oracle parameter, chosen anew for each grid and not timed. ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The work–precision study"} ns = [101, 201, 401, 801, 1601, 3201, 6401] # nested grids: each is every second point of the next wp = map(ns) do n x, clean, noisy = signal(n, 3, 0.1) B = oracle(gaussian, x, noisy, clean, Brange(n)) λ = oracle(bsk, x, noisy, clean, λrange) s = oracle(dierckx, x, noisy, clean, srange(n, 0.1)) d = oracle(cheb, x, noisy, clean, drange(n)) (err = (fit = rms(fitted(x, noisy) .- clean), gaussian = B.err, bsk = λ.err, dierckx = s.err, cheb = d.err), time = (fit = (@b fitted($x, $noisy)).time, gaussian = (@b gaussian($x, $noisy, $(B.p))).time, bsk = (@b bsk($x, $noisy, $(λ.p))).time, dierckx = (@b dierckx($x, $noisy, $(s.p))).time, cheb = (@b cheb($x, $noisy, $(d.p))).time)) end fig = Figure(size = (800, 420)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "time to smooth [s]", ylabel = "rms error") for key in keys(names) scatterlines!(ax, [w.time[key] for w in wp], [w.err[key] for w in wp]; markersize = 8, label = names[key]) end Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | rms error, σ = 0.1 | 101 | 201 | 401 | 801 | 1601 | 3201 | 6401 | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | fit_scattered (untuned) | 0.0396 | 0.0340 | 0.0230 | 0.0132 | 0.0074 | 0.0053 | 0.0037 | | Gaussian (oracle B) | 0.0474 | 0.0375 | 0.0321 | 0.0220 | 0.0142 | 0.0106 | 0.0087 | | BSplineKit cubic (oracle λ) | 0.0359 | 0.0318 | 0.0249 | 0.0177 | 0.0103 | 0.0076 | 0.0056 | | Dierckx k=5 (oracle s) | 0.0482 | 0.0371 | 0.0306 | 0.0208 | 0.0245 | 0.0151 | 0.0108 | | FastChebInterp (oracle degree) | 0.0390 | 0.0333 | 0.0181 | 0.0138 | 0.0072 | 0.0057 | 0.0043 | Every curve descends as the samples grow, and the fit's descends fastest: once the series is long enough for the cross-validation to find the smoothing, it ends below every tuned method, the polynomial included. The FITPACK spline's curve is the uneven one — it places its own knots, and how many it chooses at a given budget `s` does not vary smoothly with the data. What the time axis adds is the cost per sample of each descent. None of this is specific to a grid. The same `fit_scattered` call takes points anywhere, in any number of dimensions, and returns an interpolant with its derivatives and integrals; the [scattered-data benchmark](scattered.qmd) is that comparison, where the smoothing splines have no counterpart. --- *Rendered with Julia 1.13.3 on a Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-14700KF machine (28 threads), with ConvolutionInterpolations.jl 1.0.2, Interpolations.jl 0.16.3, BSplineKit.jl 0.19.3, Dierckx.jl 0.5.4, FastChebInterp.jl 1.3.1, NumericalIntegration.jl 0.3.4, HCubature.jl 1.8.0, QuadGK.jl 2.11.3, ScatteredInterpolation.jl 0.3.6, NaturalNeighbours.jl 1.3.6, Chairmarks.jl 1.3.1.*
